title: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities
pub: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority [2025] EWHC 1167 (Admin)
author: Mr Justice Fordham

dom.t: Citation integrity: Concern did not determine appeal

st.t: Appeal evidence: Citation concern remained secondary
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis: it treats the citation issue as a serious but expressly deferred concern, without establishing nonexistent authorities, AI involvement or a strike-out in the supplied extracts. It identifies the decisive grounds instead as insufficient evidence linking mental illness to the prolonged delay, alongside procedural and merits weaknesses.
qs: For now, I put that matter entirely to one side.

Applying the guidance of Underhill LJ from J v K, it is very clear that the sort of evidence needed, covering the relevant periods of time, so as to explain or excuse the failure to institute an appeal, is absent in this case.

st.t: Citation integrity: Concern did not determine appeal
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis: it treats the citation-integrity concern as separate from the extension decision and documents a refusal based on an extraordinary delay and conventional procedural and evidential deficiencies. It does not establish AI fabrication or provide the later strike-out reasoning.
qs: For now, I put that matter entirely to one side.
It has reliably been calculated by the SRA as 7 years 2 months and 26 days.

mo.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: Court struck out appeal grounds for fake citations
kp.d: The High Court independently struck out the grounds of appeal as an abuse of process because the appellant repeatedly cited non-existent authorities. Although the source title refers to 25 non-existent authorities, the judgment records 27 challenged citations and finds that two were wrongly criticised because they corresponded to real, though misnamed or miscited, cases.
qs: This is just the first of some 27 such authorities listed in the SRA’s Annex.
In fairness to the Appellant, I ought to record that two of the 27 are, I think, wrongly criticised.

This, in my judgment, constitutes a set of circumstances in which I should exercise – and so I will exercise – the power of the Court to strike out the grounds of appeal in this case as an abuse of process.

kp.k: Judgment does not establish that AI generated citations
kp.d: The appellant admitted that many cited cases did not exist but denied using AI or an identifiable AI source, instead attributing the material to a Google search. The judgment therefore concerns fake-authority citation and failed verification, but it does not make a factual finding that generative AI produced the authorities.
qs: He denied using AI or any source identifiable as AI.
He claimed to have simply used a Google search for “case law in support of mental health problems”.
He accepts that this case, and many other cases which he cited to this Court, do not in fact exist.

kp.k: Unverified legal research created abuse-of-process consequences
kp.d: The appellant initially said that he had not “double-verified” the authorities and later admitted that he had not checked them at all. The decision treats the absence of verification before filing and relying on legal research as serious misconduct with procedural consequences.
qs: He told me that he never “double-verified” them.
He later accepted that he never checked them at all.
There have been multiple examples of fake authorities cited by the Appellant to the Court, in these proceedings.

kp.k: Formal filing and continued reliance aggravated misconduct
kp.d: The court emphasised that the fabricated authorities appeared in formal court documents, remained relied upon, and were neither withdrawn nor explained even after the SRA identified the problem before the hearing. The finding therefore rested on continued procedural use, not merely an initial research error.
qs: The citations were included, and maintained, in formal documents before the Court.
They were never withdrawn.
They were never explained.
That, notwithstanding that they were pointed out by the SRA, well ahead of this hearing.

kp.k: Court prioritised integrity against fabricated legal authority
kp.d: Fordham J stated that courts must respond decisively to fake citations to protect the integrity of judicial processes. This is the judgment’s principal institutional recommendation and applies regardless of whether AI, search technology or another source generated the false material.
qs: In my judgment, the Court needs to take decisive action to protect the integrity of its processes against any citation of fake authority.
They are non-existent cases.
I was wholly unpersuaded by that answer.

kp.k: Former solicitor status heightened the court’s concern
kp.d: The judgment expressly considered it aggravating that the person submitting the fake authorities had previously practised as a solicitor. This connects verification failures to professional expectations attached to legally trained court users, even when they appear as litigants in person.
qs: Here, moreover, they have been put forward by someone who was previously a practising solicitor.
The case materials were rightly been prepared for the Court by the SRA as an appropriate course where the Appellant is a litigant in person, albeit a former solicitor.

kp.k: Substantive correctness could not excuse fake supporting cases
kp.d: The appellant argued that his legal propositions could remain sound even if their cited authorities did not exist. The court rejected that reasoning, indicating that potentially valid legal arguments do not neutralise the procedural seriousness of fabricated supporting authority.
qs: He claimed that the substance of the points which were being put forward in the grounds of appeal were sound, even if the authority which was being cited for those points did not exist.
He was saying, on that basis, that the citation of non-existent (fake) authorities would not be a sufficient basis to concern the Court, at least to the extent of taking that course.
I was wholly unpersuaded by that answer.

kp.k: Fake citations supported an indemnity costs sanction
kp.d: The court ordered indemnity costs of £24,727.20, payable within 21 days. Fordham J said the order marked the court’s strong disapproval of the abuse of process constituted by putting forward fake authorities, linking verification failure to substantial financial consequences.
qs: The SRA has made an application for costs on an indemnity basis, summary assessed at £24,727.20, to be paid within 21 days.

Specifically, it is based on marking the Court’s strong disapproval in relation to my finding of an abuse of the process of the court by the Appellant, in having put forward the citation of fake authorities.
In all the circumstances, the indemnity costs order is fully justified and I will make the order in the terms sought.

kp.k: SRA research exposed non-existent and miscited authorities
kp.d: The SRA and its solicitors attempted to locate the appellant’s authorities and documented the results in an annex to their skeleton argument. The court’s example showed a citation assigned to different parties and a proposition unsupported by similarly named real cases, illustrating the checking required to identify fabricated or unreliable legal research.
qs: Within the SRA’s skeleton argument (dated 6 May 2025), and addressed in detail in an Annex to that skeleton argument, there is a description of the inability of the SRA and its solicitors in locating cases that have been cited in the Appellant’s grounds of appeal and also in his own skeleton argument (21 April 2025).

The SRA’s Annex records that the SRA was unable to locate this case; that the citation was incorrect and was for a case with different parties; that cases with this name do exist; but that they do not appear to stand for the proposition given.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The judgment makes no concrete claim or prediction about AI changing legal services and does not establish that AI produced the fake authorities.
pts.d: Fordham J records that the appellant denied using AI. The relevant judicial claim is instead technology-neutral: citing and maintaining fake authorities can constitute abuse of process warranting strike-out and indemnity costs. This is a case about fabricated authorities and failure to check them, not an established instance of AI hallucination.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence concerns nonexistent authorities, rather than their technological origin.
pts.d: At paragraphs 51–53, Fordham J relies on the SRA's research annex identifying 27 problematic authorities, discounts two criticisms, examines an illustrative citation, and records the appellant's admissions that cases did not exist and that he had not checked them. The appellant attributed the material to a Google search. The judgment supplies no model identification, AI output record, benchmark, or finding establishing AI provenance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source records a 2025 judicial response to conduct in this appeal, not a forecast about AI.
pts.d: The abuse finding rests on multiple fake authorities included and maintained in formal documents by a former practising solicitor, without withdrawal or explanation despite advance notice from the SRA. The extension-of-time application was independently refused. Indemnity costs were based on the appellant's conduct since February 2024, rather than his earlier mental-health circumstances.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The demonstrated consequences affect the appellant, the responding regulator and its solicitors, and the integrity of court proceedings; no AI-specific market effects are asserted.
pts.d: The appellant, a former solicitor acting in person, had his grounds struck out and was ordered to pay indemnity costs of £24,727.20 within 21 days. The SRA and its solicitors researched the challenged citations. Fordham J framed the response as protection of the court's processes, without making broader claims about AI-driven employment, pricing, productivity, or access to justice.
